'''Faircloth:''' {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} | title = U.S. Senator | before_election = [[Lauch Faircloth]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[John Edwards]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsNC}} The '''1998 United States Senate election in North Carolina''' was held on November 3, 1998. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] incumbent [[Lauch Faircloth]] ran for re-election to a second term but was defeated by Democratic trial attorney [[John Edwards]].{{cite web |last=Clerk of the U.S. House of Representatives |author-link=Clerk of the United States House of Representatives |title=Statistics of the Congressional Election of November 3, 1998 |url=https://clerk.house.gov/member_info/electionInfo/1998election.pdf |publisher=[[U.S. Government Printing Office]] |page=33}} At 45 years of age, Edwards became the youngest elected U.S. Senator from North Carolina. Edwards later declined to run for reelection in [[2004 United States Senate election in North Carolina|2004]], choosing instead to run for [[president of the United States]]. Eventually, he was chosen as the Democratic nominee for [[Vice President of the United States|vice president]] by [[John Kerry]]. They lost to incumbents [[George W. Bush]] and [[Dick Cheney]], and Edwards later [[John Edwards 2008 presidential campaign|ran again for president in 2008]]. As of 2026, this is the last time where a Democrat won North Carolina's Class 3 Senate seat, the last time a male Democrat won a Senate seat in North Carolina until [[Roy Cooper]]'s [[2026 United States Senate election in North Carolina|victory in the state's other senate seat]], and the last time a member of the incumbent president's party unseated an incumbent in a state the party had lost in the prior presidential election.{{efn|Subsequently, the Republicans won the [[2002 United States Senate election in Minnesota]] following then-president [[George W. Bush]]'s loss in the state in [[2000 United States presidential election in Minnesota|2000]], but incumbent Democratic senator [[Paul Wellstone]] had died in a plane crash 11 days before the general election and was replaced on the ballot by [[Walter Mondale]].}} == Republican primary == In the Republican primary, Faircloth easily defeated two minor candidates.{{Cite web |title=State Board of Elections |url=http://www.app.sboe.state.nc.us/NCSBE/Elec/Results/98primry/98p143.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081127044322/http://www.app.sboe.state.nc.us/NCSBE/Elec/Results/98primry/98p143.pdf |archive-date=2008-11-27 |access-date=2010-06-28}} == Democratic primary == === Candidates === * Bob Ayers Jr. * James Carmack * [[John Edwards]], Raleigh attorney * Gene Gay * [[D. G. Martin]], former vice chancellor of the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] * Mike Robinson * Ella Scarborough, former member of the [[Charlotte City Council]] ==== Declined ==== * [[Mike Easley]], [[North Carolina Attorney General|North Carolina attorney general]] since 1993 * [[Harvey Gantt]], former mayor of [[Charlotte, North Carolina|Charlotte]] and 1990 and 1996 nominee for Senate * Mike Robinson, [[Davidson County, North Carolina|Davidson County]] businessman * Charlie Sanders, former CEO of [[GSK plc|Glaxo]] and candidate for Senate in 1996 Going into the 1998 campaign, several prominent Democrats declined to run for Senate, including [[Mike Easley]], [[Harvey Gantt]], and Charlie Sanders.{{Cite web|title=EDWARDS SHOULD LEAD THE DEMOCRATIC TICKET\|url=https://greensboro.com/edwards-should-lead-the-democratic-ticket/article_a3684e65-a17c-5dfb-a2d4-d30a8b317bbc.html|access-date=2022-02-13|website=Greensboro News and Record|date=May 1998 |language=en}} === Results === In the Democratic primary, Edwards defeated his closest rival [[D.G. Martin]], former vice chancellor of the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]]. * [[John Edwards]], Raleigh attorney (Democratic) * Barbara Howe (Libertarian) * [[Lauch Faircloth]], incumbent U.S. senator since 1993 (Republican) === Campaign === During the campaign, Edwards fashioned himself as a "people's advocate", while Faircloth accused Edwards of being too friendly towards labor unions.{{Cite news|last=Dewar|first=Helen|date=July 11, 1998|title=North Carolina's Stark Clash|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/politics/campaigns/keyraces98/stories/nc071198.htm|access-date=2022-02-13|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]}} Referring to Edwards as a "tobacco-taxing liberal", Faircloth's campaign ran ads alleging that Edwards' position on [[tobacco]] regulation would lead to job losses in the state.{{Cite web|last=Andron|first=Scott|title=ATTACK ADS SIGNIFY CLOSE SENATE RACE\ SENATE CANDIDATES JOHN EDWARDS AND LAUCH FAIRCLOTH ACCUSE EACH OTHER OF LYING ABOUT EDWARDS' STANDS ON TOBACCO.|url=https://greensboro.com/attack-ads-signify-close-senate-race-senate-candidates-john-edwards-and-lauch-faircloth-accuse-each/article_435ac810-49be-5d25-8671-8c1965099a0f.html|access-date=2022-02-13|website=Greensboro News and Record|date=26 October 1998 |language=en}} Edwards' campaign refused financial support from [[political action committee]]s and ran ads criticizing Faircloth's record on [[Medicare (United States)|Medicare]] and [[Social Security (United States)|Social Security]].{{Cite web|title=North Carolina Senate - November 3, 1998|url=https://www.cnn.com/ALLPOLITICS/stories/1998/11/03/election/senate/north.carolina/|access-date=2022-02-13|website=[[CNN]]}} Edwards' victory was partially attributed by some observers to blowback against the Faircloth campaign's use of negative advertising.{{Cite news|last=Bragg|first=Rick|date=1998-11-06|title=THE 1998 ELECTION: THE DISCONTENTED; Rejecting Negative Advertising, and the Candidate|language=en-US|work=The New York
